newsitem.title: BOSNIA: "Sacked' Bosnian Serb police chief resurfaces.
newsitem.headline: "Sacked' Bosnian Serb police chief resurfaces.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb police chief who NATO and the U.N. thought had been sacked two months ago at their insistence appears to be still in office, a U.N. spokesman said on Tuesday.

The head of U.N. police monitors in postwar Bosnia has demanded an explanation from the Serb interior minister after reports that Simo Drljaca still held senior law enforcement duties in the northern district of Prijedor.

Human-rights investigators say Drljaca led Serb nationalist paramilitary units in a campaign of terror and ethnic expulsions of local Moslems and Croats in the Prijedor area early in Bosnia's 1992-95 war.

He was supposedly fired as police chief after NATO issued an ultimatum for his removal in the wake of an incident in which Drljaca and some of his men menaced peacekeepers with submachine guns banned under a demilitarisation regime.

"(We are) concerned by recent reports that the former chief of police of Prijedor appears to be working in an official capacity in the Prijedor security station," said Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force (IPTF).
"He has been observed by IPTF monitors in meetings with police officials, working inside the security centre and travelling and operating police vehicles," Ivanko said.

"In addition, we have reports that he has made statements to the local media that he continues to control the (local) police and that he now holds a senior position within the ministry of internal affairs," he told a news conference.

Ivanko said IPTF Commissioner Peter Fitzgerald had written to Bosnian Serb Interior Minister Dragan Kijac demanding Drljaca's unequivocal dismissal from any law-enforcement post if indeed he still held any.
Western observers regard the Prijedor police force as one of the more disreputable in the Serb republic entity of Bosnia.
Last week, international peace coordinators discovered that four policemen on the force were on the indictment roster of the international tribunal on war crimes in former Yugoslavia.

John Shattuck, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for human rights, told reporters in Sarajevo on Monday that Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic promised him in talks on Sunday that the four would be fired.

But he said Plavsic baulked at fulfilling the Serbs' obligation under the 1995 Dayton peace treaty to surrender the four and other Serb indictees -- there are more than 50 -- to the tribunal for trial in The Hague.
